question_en: With respect to cumulative preference shares, dividends that were not paid in prior periods are most likely:
option_a: forfeited and not paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future.
option_b: accrued and paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future before paying common shareholders.
option_c: accrued and paid to cumulative preference shareholders in the future only after paying
explanation_en:
Types of preference shares (preferred stock)
Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid
Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods
Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold
Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance
Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares
Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price
Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price
Preferred (preference) shares ownership represents a form of equity investment in a company. Preference shares may grant certain benefits to
preferred shareholders such as high dividend payments and in some cases conversion rights (to common stock). Furthermore, dividend
payments to preferred shareholders take precedence over dividend payments to common shareholders. Preferred dividends can be cumulative
or noncumulative.
For cumulative preference dividends, if a company does not pay a dividend (or dividends) in one period (or several periods), the unpaid dividend
accrues and is owed in the future. Conversely, for noncumulative preference dividends, the company does not accrue (and does not owe payment
for) unpaid dividends from past periods.
(Choice A) Unpaid dividends on cumulative preferred shares are accrued and owed to preferred shareholders.
(Choice C) Payments of past unpaid dividends are due to preference shareholders before any dividends can be distributed to common
shareholders.

question_en: In contrast to statutory voting, cumulative voting allows common shareholders to cast:
explanation_en:
Shareholders often vote in board of director elections, which are conducted via statutory voting or cumulative voting. Often, one vote is tied to
each share.
In the case of statutory voting, shareholders must allocate their total votes, which are based on the number of open board seats, evenly among
the candidates. Under this system, larger shareholders have greater representation than smaller shareholders. In cumulative voting,
shareholders can disproportionally allocate their votes to any one candidate (or any number of candidates), which can improve representation
for smaller shareholders.
In the example above, three board seats are open for election and there are five candidates. Suppose a particular shareholder has 300 votes.
Under statutory voting, the shareholder must pick three candidates and distribute 100 votes to each of the three. Under cumulative voting, the
shareholder can apply all 300 votes to one candidate. This benefits the shareholder if this shareholder strongly prefers a specific candidate to win
a board seat.
(Choice A) A cumulative voting system does not change the total number of votes granted to a shareholder.
(Choice C) Each vote is cast for one candidate. A single vote cannot be split for multiple candidates.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a feature of preference shares?
option_a: Call features allow issuers the right to buy back shares from investors.
option_b: Convertible shares allow shareholders to convert shares into subordinated debt.
option_c: Participating shares provide shareholders the same voting rights as common shares.
explanation_en:
Types of preference shares (preferred stock)
Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid
Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods
Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold
Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance
Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares
Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price
Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price
Preference (ie, preferred) shares are a type of equity security. Compared to common shares, preference shares often have larger (but fixed)
dividends, as well as higher priority over dividend payments and residual claims on a company's assets.
There are several types of preference shares (shown in the table above). If preference shares are callable, they have an embedded call option
that gives the issuing company (ie, issuer) the right to buy back shares from investors at a predetermined call price.
(Choice B) Convertible shares allow shareholders to convert their shares into common stock, not subordinated debt.
(Choice C) Participating shares provide shareholders the opportunity to earn additional dividend payments if a company's profits exceed a
predetermined threshold. They do not provide voting rights.

question_en: A demand analysis of a company's product should most likely consider:
explanation_en: Analysis of company products and services Market size Product differentiation Demand Economic and demographic factors Opportunities Input sources Capacity Supply Import/export considerations Proprietary products An analysis of demand is conducted to estimate a firm's current and future revenue. Factors considered include the following: Size of the market: Potential unit sales and prices and forecasted rates of change Industry product: Either differentiated (eg, make/model of automobiles) or homogeneous (eg, mobile phone service) External influences: Sensitivity of industry revenues to changes in the economy (eg, GDP growth), demographics (eg, age distribution of population), and social attitudes (eg, tobacco use, income inequality) Business opportunities: Revenue potential from introducing new products or entering new markets Product differentiation among competitors relates to the analysis of demand. When competitors sell undifferentiated products, price competition is more intense. Firms operating in such commoditized markets have little pricing power. If products differ among competitors (ie, differentiated products), demand is more stable, and firms tend to have more pricing power. If products are not qualitatively different, firms attempt to achieve differentiation through advertising and trademarks to promote brand loyalty. (Choices A and B) Company capacity and cost structure and industry concentration are considered when analyzing supply.

question_en: A company is developing a product for planned launch in 20X8. An analyst collects the company's 20X7 actual financial data and creates 20X8 forecasts for two scenarios: The company's degree of operating leverage in 20X8 will most likely be:
option_a: greater if the new product launches in 20X8.
option_b: the same regardless of whether the new product launches.
option_c: greater if the new product does not launch in 20X8.
explanation_en: Operating leverage refers to the level of fixed costs in a company's cost structure. Increasing fixed costs relative to variable costs increases operating leverage. The degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures the rate at which operating profit increases (decreases) relative to the rate at which sales increase (decrease). The greater (smaller) a company's operating leverage, the more (less) operating income will change given a change in sales. A company's DOL may differ from its peers' depending on its cost structure, and a single company's DOL can change over time. In this scenario, the company's DOL must be calculated and compared for two separate scenarios: If the company launches a new product If the company does not launch a new product The company's DOL under each scenario can be calculated as: In both scenarios, the percentage change in operating income is twice the percentage change in sales, so the company's DOL is the same (Choices A and C). Note, however, that this may not always be the case, such as if the new product had a greater or lesser contribution margin or fixed cost requirements than the overall company, all else equal.

question_en: Which of the following metrics should most appropriately be considered in top-down revenue analysis for a restaurant company? The company's:
explanation_en: Forecasting a company's financials (eg, revenue, working capital) can be done using a top-down, bottom-up, or hybrid approach. A top-down approach starts by identifying factors that can affect growth in the overall economy, sector, or industry in which the company operates and then applies those factors to company-specific forecasts. A bottom-up approach starts with features of the company or a segment of the company (eg, product, geography) and uses company- specific historical ratios or growth rates to construct forecasts by assuming a continuation of, or a change in, a trend. Analysts will often use a combination of both approaches, which can be useful for uncovering biases or errors that may arise from using only one approach. Common top-down approaches use GDP growth or market size and market share. Using market size and market share, an analyst forecasts the total size of the relevant market, then estimates the company's market share over time. Therefore, the restaurant company's market share would be a relevant metric for a top-down analysis. (Choices B and C) The number of restaurants and average revenue per seat are company-specific metrics that would be more relevant for a bottom-up approach.

question_en: Which of the following companies is most likely to have pricing power? A:
option_a: low-cost producer in the competitive textile market.
option_b: consumer goods producer with a popular brand name.
option_c: global manufacturer of low-cost personal computer accessories.
explanation_en: An analysis of a company's financials usually begins with revenue, and price is a key component of revenue. Pricing power is a company's ability to increase prices without significantly affecting its unit volumes of sales. A company with greater pricing power can raise prices without significantly lowering sales volume (ie, demand is less elastic). Pricing pressure is typically lower in perfectly competitive markets and higher in other industry structures. Industries in which companies have pricing power are often marked by one or more of the following: Product differentiation High barriers to entry Few economical substitutes High switching costs for customers High customer loyalty and retention Companies with strong brand names typically have higher customer loyalty and can therefore increase prices without a significant impact on volumes. Thus, a consumer goods producer with a popular brand name (eg, Coca-Cola) is most likely to have pricing power. (Choice A) A low-cost producer has lower costs than some competitors and therefore can earn an accounting profit even in a perfectly competitive market. Still, a company in such a market would not be able to increase prices without losing a significant portion of its customer base. Therefore, a low-cost producer in the competitive textile market would not likely have pricing power. (Choice C) Commoditization occurs when an original product is no longer unique due to competitors entering the market with similar products. For instance, the market for personal computer accessories is a commoditized market with many competitors and little product differentiation, so a low-cost global producer in that market would not have pricing power.

question_en: Which of the following statements best describes an aspect of spreadsheet modeling for company analysis?
option_a: A more complex model leads to more accurate analysis.
option_b: A complex model can lead to a false sense of confidence.
option_c: A standardized model should be applied to all companies.
explanation_en: Spreadsheet modeling has become a nearly universal tool in financial statement analysis. A complex model can lead to a false sense of confidence in the precision of the model output. Complex spreadsheet models are highly dependent on numerous forecasts and assumptions. Therefore, the risk of error is high, and such errors can quickly compound, creating increasingly inaccurate outputs. At the same time, the model's complexity can encourage overconfidence in its precision. Once a model is complete, a reality check should be performed by testing for reasonableness. Only a handful of critical drivers should materially impact the bottom-line results. (Choice A) Increasingly complex models do not necessarily produce better outputs and often lead to a false sense of confidence in the precision of the model's output. (Choice C) Spreadsheet models should closely match the financial reporting and disclosures of the company being analyzed. This allows for direct comparisons between the model and what was reported by the company. While a standardized model may have some benefits regarding consistency, the comparability of forecasts and assumptions for each individual company could be negatively impacted.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely a source of capital for a company?
explanation_en: Sources and uses of capital Sources Uses Cash flows from operations Cash and investments Net working capital (negative) Net working capital (positive) Debt issuance Capital expenditures Equity issuance Intangible asset purchases Asset disposal Acquisitions Debt paydown Dividends Share repurchases Company research typically involves identifying and analyzing sources and uses of capital. Evaluating trends over time and comparing company data with peers can help analysts identify strengths and weaknesses or competitive advantages and disadvantages. Sources of capital are any activities that generate capital to fund operating, investing, and financing activities. Uses of capital are activities that invest in operations, including capital expenditures, or that return capital to stakeholders. A company's capital is commonly sourced from operations (ie, cash flow from operations) and from third parties (eg, issuance of equity or debt). However, sources of capital also include one-time infusions, such as asset disposals or sales. (Choices B and C) Cash and investments and positive net working capital are uses of capital. Cash and investments are used to maintain liquidity for business operations, interest payments, or other items. Positive net working capital is used to support operations.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.05 Company Analysis Past and Present - Answers.pdf
question_en: A nonbank company increases the amount of debt in its capital structure. All else equal, this will most likely affect the company's:
explanation_en: In addition to measuring operating risks, analysts typically evaluate a company's risks related to its capital structure (ie, financial risk). Larger amounts of debt in a company's capital structure will increase the company's obligated principal and interest payments, and therefore its financial risk. The degree of financial leverage (DFL), which is the rate of change in a company's net income compared with the change in its operating income, measures this risk. A company's DFL is directly affected by interest expense. Interest expense is a nonoperating cost and therefore affects net income, but not operating income. Larger interest payments result in a larger DFL, thus making net income more sensitive to changes in operating income since the company has a riskier capital structure that relies more on debt financing. A DFL close to 1 indicates there is little interest expense as the company largely uses equity financing. (Choice A) Contribution margin is the difference between a product's unit price and unit variable costs. For a nonbank company, contribution margin would be unaffected by increases in the amount of debt in a company's capital structure. (Choice C) Degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures the rate that operating profit increases (decreases) in relation to sales increases (decreases). For nonbank companies, DOL is affected by the company's operating cost structure (ie, fixed versus variable costs) but would not be impacted by changes in interest rates.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.05 Company Analysis Past and Present - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best demonstrates pricing power?
explanation_en: Pricing power Attributes that affect pricing power Indicators of pricing power Product differentiation Barriers to entry Lack of substitutes Rising margins and profitability Switching costs Customer loyalty Price is a key component of a company's revenue. Pricing power is a company's ability to increase prices without causing sales volume to decline significantly. A company with greater (less) pricing power can (cannot) raise prices without meaningfully affecting demand. A company's pricing power is largely determined by both the industry structure and the company's competitive positioning within the market. One indicator of pricing power is the ability to pass on cost increases to customers by increasing price. Analysts can evaluate a company's pricing power by comparing its pricing trends to its cost trends: if prices cannot keep pace with costs—in other words, if profit margins (eg, operating margin, net margin) are shrinking—then the company has little pricing power. Expanding profit margins indicate that a company has significant pricing power: it can raise prices faster than costs rise, without fear of substitutes or competitors taking market share with lower prices. (Choice A) Gaining market share does not demonstrate pricing power. For instance, the company could be lowering prices to increase volume, which is not an example of pricing power and may not be sustainable. (Choice C) Consistently growing revenue alone does not demonstrate pricing power since costs may be growing even faster than revenue.

question_en: A consumer bank expands its offerings to include brokerage and asset management services. As these offerings expand, the bank's profit margin improves. This is best described as:
explanation_en: Companies can often improve their cost structure over time by increasing the size of their business or adding related business lines. Economies of scope occur when companies reduce their average cost per unit by increasing the number of business lines or products offered. Efficiencies typically result from cost-sharing between businesses (eg, financial service firms sharing back-office functions and cross-selling services) or an ability to use fixed costs for multiple functions (eg, passenger airplanes carrying freight cargo). Economies of scale occur when companies reduce their average cost per unit by increasing the quantity produced. Some reasons why companies might experience economies of scale include: Greater bargaining power with suppliers Ability to spread fixed costs over more units Availability of new efficiencies (eg, in marketing) Lower cost of capital As average cost per unit declines, profit margins typically expand, assuming prices remain stable. In this scenario, the bank's profit margins expand as it adds new product offerings. This describes economies of scope. (Choice A) The bank's margins are expanding due to new business lines, not greater quantity (ie, scale of output) for its traditional products or services. (Choice C) Degree of financial leverage (DFL) is the rate at which net income changes compared with changes in operating income. DFL is directly affected by interest expense and is not related to a company's expanding operating margins due to scale or scope.

question_en:
An analyst collects the following data for a company:

| ($ millions) 20X3 |  | 20X4 |
|---|---|---|
| Sales 600 |  | 900 |
| COGS 350 |  | 600 |
| Fixed operating costs | 90 | 100 |
| Interest expense | 80 | 90 |
| Tax expense | 20 | 25 |

The company's degree of financial leverage is closest to:
explanation_en: Risks related to a company's capital structure (ie, financial risk) can be measured using solvency ratios, third-party credit ratings, and the degree of financial leverage (DFL). A company's DFL measures the rate of change in its net income compared with a change in operating income. All else equal, increasing interest expense, which is a nonoperating cost driven by debt, will reduce net income but not affect operating income. Therefore, when net income is positive, greater interest expense causes net income to change at a faster rate than operating income, causing the DFL to increase. In this scenario, the company's operating income and net income in each period must be calculated before the DFL: The company's DFL is approximately 1.67. (Choice A) 0.50 is the company's degree of operating leverage, which is driven by fixed operating costs. (Choice B) 0.83 is the company's degree of total leverage, which is driven by both fixed operating costs and financing costs.

question_en: A firm has reported negative net working capital for each of the past four quarters. Based only on this, an analyst can most appropriately infer that the firm is:
option_a: not profiting from its marginal output.
option_c: relying on suppliers as a source of financing.
explanation_en: Working capital management Net working capital Sources of financing Negative Current liabilities > Current assets Assets plus external, including suppliers Positive Current liabilities < Current assets Assets Along with fixed capital, working capitalrequirements determine the amount of investment a company requires to maintain its operations. Greater working capital requirements mean less funds are available for other uses, such as distributions to shareholders or debt retirement. If working capital is positive, current assets exceed current liabilities, and the company can meet current obligations. If working capital is negative, the company's current assets are less than (and therefore cannot support) its current liabilities; in essence, the company is using its suppliers as a source of short-term financing. (Choice A) The profit or loss from marginal output is determined by its contribution margin (= Price – Variable cost) and is not directly affected by working capital. (Choice B) A report of positive or negative working capital does not provide any detail as to whether a company is shortening or lengthening its cash conversion cycle, which is reflected in activity ratios.

question_en: When conducting a company analysis, which of the following factors is least useful for analyzing supply?
explanation_en: Analysis of company products and services Market size Product differentiation Demand Economic and demographic factors Opportunities Input sources Capacity Supply Import/export considerations Proprietary products Part of a thorough company analysis is an analysis of the company's ability to supply product to customers. This ability is influenced by competition for resources and production capacity within the industry. Factors in supply analysis include: Input sources—Competition or concentration in industries that supply inputs, and availability of substitute resources Industry capacity—Current capacity and anticipated expansions, and the ease or difficulty of adding capacity Firm capacity—Output potential and cost structure International factors—Potential impact of import competition on supply and prices in the product market; impact on input prices from exports to foreign competitors Proprietary products and trademarks—Possibility of restraining output below capacity to maintain the value of products and trademarks Product differentiation across the industry indicates the degree of competition for the company's product. It is a factor in analyzing demand for the product, not supply. (Choice B) An anticipated expansion of industry capacity affects the industry's ability to offer products to customers and is a factor in analyzing company supply. (Choice C) Price competition between resource suppliers affects a company's cost structure and is a factor in analyzing company supply.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.05 Company Analysis Past and Present - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best approximates contribution margin?
explanation_en: A company's contribution margin is the difference between its unit price and unit variable costs and measures the approximate contribution to profit from each incremental unit sold. When price exceeds variable costs, each marginal unit produced will create additional profit for the company. When the company produces a great enough quantity, the contribution profit will exceed fixed operating costs and operating profit will become positive. For most companies, a significant portion of costs of goods sold (COGS) incurred during a period is variable (eg, material, freight, and storage costs). A significant portion of total COGS varies with the number of units produced or sold. Therefore, COGS tends to be a suitable approximation of a company's total variable costs. Gross margin is the difference between revenue and COGS; therefore, it is a suitable approximation of contribution margin. (Choices B and C) Costs that go into a company's operating and EBITDA margins, but not in gross margin, include sales & marketing, general & administrative (G&A), and research & development (R&D). These (eg, salaries, marketing, rent) tend to be more fixed in nature and therefore operating and EBITDA margins would not make good approximations for contribution margin.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.05 Company Analysis Past and Present - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst collects the following information on a company and its industry peers: Based only on this information, the most appropriate conclusion is that the company:
option_a: has a better credit rating than peers.
option_c: generates returns that exceed equity investors' requirements.
explanation_en: Return on equity (ROE) measures how much profit a company generates relative to its equity. ROE is often compared with investors' required rate of return (r) to determine whether the company is generating profit in excess of the return required by its equity investors. When ROE is greater (less) than r, the company is generating a profit that exceeds (falls short of) what is required by investors. DuPont analysis decomposes ROE into measures of profitability, efficiency, and leverage. ROE is the product of the company's profit margin, asset turnover, and leverage ratio (ie, equity multiplier). In this scenario, using the three ratios, the company's ROE can be calculated as 0.04 × 1.2 × 2.5 = 0.12 = 12%, which exceeds the required return on equity of 9%. (Choice A) The company and its peers are in the same industry, yet its cost of debt (6%) exceeds the industry average of 5%. Although a credit rating is based on many factors, this greater cost of debt suggests that the company would have a worse credit rating than its industry peers. (Choice B) The company has an equity multiplier of 2.5 and degree of financial leverage of 2, suggesting a significant amount of debt in its capital structure and therefore higher financial risk. It would not be appropriate to assume that the company has a conservative capital structure.

question_en: A clothing manufacturer has two business segments: ● Its retail segment designs and manufactures clothes that it sells to retailers. ● Its merchant segment manufactures clothing for other designers and earns commissions when the designers sell to retailers. Which of the following best describes the customer base for the company's merchant segment?
explanation_en: The first step to analyze a company is to assess its business model. Business model analysis provides a basis for determining the drivers of the company's financials and its opportunities and risks; this gives the analyst direction on where to focus additional research. Elements of a business model analysis include identifying the customer and key customer groups. This identification will provide insight into the addressable market and whether the customer base is large or small, diverse or homogeneous, and concentrated or fragmented. A company sells its products or services directly to customers, so customers are the party that directly purchases from the company. A customer can repackage or add additional value to a product or service, then resell it to its own customer. Companies may also have different categories of customers. In this scenario, the company's retail segment manufactures and designs clothes that it sells directly to retailers, who resell the clothes to consumers. The company also has a merchant segment that manufactures clothes for designers in exchange for commissions paid when the designers sell the clothes to retailers. For the retail segment, the customers are retailers. For the merchant segment, the customers are designers, who receive the company's manufacturing services and pay commissions when they sell the clothes to retailers; through the commissions, the designers purchase directly from the company. (Choice B) Retailers are the designers' customer base, not the merchant segment's. (Choice C) Clothing consumers are the retailers' customer base, not the merchant segment's.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.05 Company Analysis Past and Present - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company purchases a piece of equipment that reduces its need for temporary labor, thus increasing its fixed costs as a percentage of total costs. All else equal, the company's degree of operating leverage will most likely:
explanation_en: For a firm with fixed costs to be profitable, its contribution margin (= P − VC) must remain positive and greater than its fixed costs, so that operating profit (= Q(P − VC) − FC) is positive: If FC > 0, then P − VC > 0 and P − VC > FC, and as a result, Q(P − VC) − FC > 0. P = Price per unit VC = Variable cost per unit FC = Fixed cost Q = Quantity sold Operating leverage refers to the proportion of fixed costs in a company's cost structure. Holding other factors constant, a company that increases fixed costs as a percentage of total costs will increase the rate at which operating profit changes. When the proportion of fixed costs increases and: contribution margin is positive, operating income will increase (decrease) faster as quantity increases (decreases). contribution margin is negative, operating income will decrease (increase) faster as quantity increases (decreases). The degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures the rate that operating profit increases (decreases) relative to increases (decreases) in sales. Since a greater proportion of fixed costs will increase the rate that operating profit changes for a given change in quantity, it will also increase the DOL, all else equal. Therefore, a firm that reduces a variable cost such as temporary labor while increasing a fixed cost such as equipment, all else equal, will report an increase to its DOL (Choices A and B).
